title: Train/Test/Validation Splits
summary: Learn how to split data so evaluation is honest — train/validation/test, cross-validation, and the leakage bugs that silently invalidate both.

slides.markdown: A model's reported number is only as trustworthy as how it was measured. This topic covers why training accuracy lies, what train/validation/test each protect, how k-fold and nested cross-validation avoid wasting data, and the specific leakage bugs — temporal, target, preprocessing — that quietly invalidate a benchmark. Split wrong, and a model can look great in the notebook and fail on day one in production.

slides.subTitle: Memorization vs generalization
slides.markdown: A model graded on the data it trained on isn't being evaluated — it's reciting an answer key. Given enough capacity, a model can **memorize** training examples, including their noise, instead of learning the general pattern — so training accuracy looks excellent even for a model that fails on anything new. A student scoring 100% on questions they've already seen the answers to hasn't proven understanding, just recall. **Generalization**, not recall, is what evaluation is supposed to measure.

slides.subTitle: Train, validation, test
slides.markdown: Split data into three disjoint sets, each with one job: **train** fits the model's parameters; **validation** compares model variants and tunes hyperparameters, feeding back into more training; **test** is touched exactly once, at the very end, to report the number you'll actually trust. A common ratio is 60/20/20, but the real rule is: never let test-set performance influence a single decision before that final check — the moment it does, it stops measuring generalization and starts measuring fit to the test set.

With limited data, one validation split wastes data and its score depends on which rows landed where. **K-fold cross-validation** fixes both:

![5-fold cross-validation: train on 4 folds, validate on the rotating held-out fold](assets/k-fold-cv.svg)

Split data into k equal folds; train k times, holding out a different fold each time; average the k scores into one stable estimate. Every row is validated on exactly once.

slides.subTitle: Temporal, target, and preprocessing leaks
slides.markdown: **Data leakage** is when information from outside the training set — often from the future or from the label itself — sneaks in and inflates the score. Three common types: **temporal leakage** (using data that wouldn't exist yet at prediction time); **target leakage** (a feature that's a disguised copy of the label, e.g. a field that's only set once the outcome is known); **preprocessing leakage** (fitting a scaler or imputer on the full dataset before splitting, so test-set statistics bleed into training). All three produce great validation scores that don't survive production.

slides.subTitle: Hold-out vs cross-validation vs time-based split
slides.markdown:
Which strategy is right depends on your data's volume and structure.

| Strategy | Best when | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Hold-out (single split) | Large dataset, fast iteration | Score depends on the lucky/unlucky split |
| K-fold cross-validation | Small/medium dataset, need stability | k times slower to run |
| Time-based split | Data has a time order (forecasting, fraud) | Random k-fold here leaks the future |

Default to hold-out when data is abundant; reach for cross-validation when data is scarce; always use a time-based split when order matters.

slides.subTitle: Keeping rare classes represented
slides.markdown: When one class is rare — say 2% fraud in a dataset — a plain random split can accidentally starve validation or test of positive examples, making the reported score meaningless or wildly noisy across reruns. **Stratified sampling** fixes this by splitting each class separately, so every split preserves the original class ratio. A 2% fraud rate in the full dataset means roughly 2% fraud in train, validation, and test alike — not 0% in one split by bad luck.

slides.subTitle: Shuffling time-series data
slides.markdown: Shuffling rows before splitting is the default in most tooling — and it's exactly wrong for time-series data. Shuffle first and the model trains on data from **after** the point it's tested on, effectively peeking at the future; a forecasting model can look highly accurate in validation, then fail completely once deployed, because in production it never gets to see ahead. For time-ordered data, always split by a fixed cutoff date — train on the past, validate and test on the future — and never shuffle first.

slides.subTitle: Tuning without leaking into the final score
slides.markdown: Tuning hyperparameters on the same cross-validation folds you use to report the final score leaks information — you've implicitly picked whatever did best on the very data you're reporting on. **Nested cross-validation** fixes this with two loops: an outer loop that holds out a fold purely for the final unbiased score, and an inner loop, run only on the outer loop's training portion, that tunes hyperparameters via its own cross-validation. It costs more compute but is the only setup that both tunes and reports honestly.

slides.subTitle: train_test_split and StratifiedKFold
slides.markdown:
Two calls to recognize on sight:

```python
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, StratifiedKFold

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42
)

skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
for train_idx, val_idx in skf.split(X, y):
    ...
```

`stratify=y` preserves class ratios in a single split; `StratifiedKFold` does the same across all k folds, not just one.
